Filed from the same formal-methods survey (2026-09-06) as its sibling, the admission random walk. That card is sequential by construction and cannot see interleavings; this card is the concurrent half. Charter sections extended: SEED-NEXT.md II.1 (freshness, the monotonic-head rule, non-fast-forward refusal on the ledger ref), II.1 genesis and halt (halt enforced at the admission boundary, not by the writer's client), and III.A row 7's race drill. No Part III row changes; not schedulable ahead of an open Phase 13 row.

WHAT EXISTS. internal/gitref/loop.go AppendLoop: fetch, materialize, verify, re-link, re-sign, push, with ErrStaleTree and ErrNonFastForward retried up to maxAttempts and ErrHeadRegression refused before any attempt (gitref.go Fetch, the monotonic-head rule). internal/halt StateAt and Check. The race drill in internal/gitref/gitref_test.go runs two concurrent appenders against a bare remote and observes a real retry. The perf gate runs 24 writers. These are executions, not enumerations: they show the loop survives the interleavings the scheduler happened to produce.

THE GAP. No test enumerates interleavings. The properties the charter states about the append protocol are interleaving properties: no lost update; every admitted record's prev was the remote tip at the moment of admission; a client's persisted verified head never regresses across any sequence of fetches, refusals and retries; a writer holding a pre-halt tip is refused at the boundary whatever its client does; the loop terminates under bounded attempts with fair scheduling and reports the typed remote rejection when it does not. For three writers and three attempts the space is small enough to walk exhaustively, and a walk is evidence a two-appender run is not.

WHAT THIS CARD OWES. An abstract state machine of the append protocol and a checker that enumerates every interleaving for small N, asserting the five properties above as invariants and producing the offending trace as the failure message. Actors: N writers, one remote holding a ref with fast-forward-only semantics, one halt-capable operator. Steps are the loop's own: fetch (with head persistence and the regression refusal), attempt (validate against the fetched tip, relink on stale tree), push (refused unless fast-forward), and the operator's halt.declared and halt.lifted. The model treats admission as a yes/no oracle; the rules inside it are the sibling card's.

TOOLCHAIN, DECIDED PER THE PLAN'S RUBRIC. Binding default: Go-native. Write the state machine and an exhaustive depth-first explorer in Go, in the next module, under make check-next at small N. This keeps the build plan's single-toolchain default (docs/next-build-plan.md section 1, language and layout) and the explorer for this state space is a couple hundred lines. TLA+ with TLC is the alternative if the model outgrows that: if the plan reaches for it, the spec lives under next/spec/ with a last-verified stamp (charter II.15), runs on the scheduled job or by hand, and never enters make check-next as a second toolchain. Lean 4 is ruled out for the reason in the survey: a proof about a model, no extraction to the code that enforces.

The plan decides: N and attempt bounds under the fast gate versus the scheduled run; whether the model's initial states are seeded from the sibling's generator (yes, if that card has merged; otherwise a fixed preamble and a follow-up to reuse it); how the model is kept honest against loop.go (candidates: the model's step names cite the loop's error values and a test asserts the set of retryable errors matches; or the drill in gitref_test.go replays a model trace against the real remote and expects the same outcome).

FOLLOW-ON, NOT THIS CARD. The same explorer over the verdict-then-merge reconciliation (verdict.rendered, merge.requested, merge.observed with the forge as a separate process; every class in internal/reconcile reachable and flagged, nothing else reachable) and over racing mode (claims below the cap, first verified success settles, the reaper clears the rest). File once this card's explorer exists and its shape is known.

Filed from a formal-methods survey (2026-09-06) that asked whether Lean 4 belongs in Seed and answered no: a proof would be about a model of internal/admit, never about the Go rule set that enforces. What the survey found worth building instead is this card and its sibling (the interleaving check). Charter section extended: SEED-NEXT.md III.I (affordances and admission share one rule set) and the section I.2 ceiling as it lands in admission. No Part III row changes; this card may not be scheduled ahead of an open Phase 13 row (docs/next-build-plan.md section 3, filable-now rule).

WHAT EXISTS. internal/admit/soundness_test.go makes the III.I regression class executable: at every prefix of one hand-written walk (walkScript in affordances_test.go), for every enrolled lane, the listed set is sorted and deterministic and every listed verb admits when independently re-drafted. internal/history generates a seeded, byte-deterministic chain, but every contract follows the same ten-record happy path (RecordsPerContract). internal/redteam loads the section I.2 ceiling as a clause table from the charter's own words and drills it clause by clause against the real hook. internal/simulate/audit.go judges any chain against five bars and returns evidence lists, never a boolean.

THE GAP. Every generator walks a scripted shape. Rule interactions at positions no script reaches are tested only where someone thought of the case: park then reclaim under halt, an escalation raised while a request is unanswered, a verdict on a returned contract, racing mode with a reap mid-flight, a budget refusal at a spending gate inside a race. admit.go is about 2,500 lines with some thirty refusal kinds, and refusal ordering is where position-stamped refusals have already needed review fixes (#84, #93, #98). Nothing explores the state space.

WHAT THIS CARD OWES. A seeded random walker in internal/admit that starts from a generated preamble and, at each position, picks an enrolled lane at random, reads its affordances at that position, and drafts either a listed verb or, some declared fraction of the time, a verb the transition table (next/spec/transitions.json) forbids at the subject's current state. It runs the enforcing Check and folds the result. Four oracles:
1. A listed verb admits (the III.I class over random positions, not one script).
2. A table-forbidden verb refuses with the transition rule's reason, not a later rule's (refusal ordering is the property).
3. The fold's state after each admission equals the table's `to` for that verb.
4. At the end of the walk the chain passes simulate.Audit clean, and the redteam clause table read as predicates over the chain holds: no done without a key-disjoint verdict, no fence out of order, no spend outside a reservation, no self-approval.

Shrinking is prefix truncation: a failure is positioned, so the minimal case is the shortest failing prefix. No shrinking library; testing/quick is too weak and rapid would be a new dependency on a module that has four. The seed is logged on failure so a red run replays.

Budget follows the perf-storm pattern: a small iteration count under make check-next (state the wall-clock budget in the plan), the large count on the scheduled run.

The plan decides: where the randomized generator lives (a Shape or random mode on history.Spec, which already carries Seed, is the obvious seam, and the sibling card reuses it); the forbidden-verb fraction; which lanes the walker plays (all six, or work lanes only with the operator verbs scripted); and whether the ceiling predicates are derived from redteam's Clause table or written beside it (derive, unless the table's vocabulary does not name a predicate).

NOT THIS CARD. Concurrency. The walker feeds one event at a time; two writers in flight is the sibling card's, which inherits this card's generator and predicates.

title: 'next: four review fixes for the worker loop (identity, contention, fence, packet leak)'
state: done

Four review findings on #191 (Phase 9 item 1c), all verified correct
against the code, arriving after that PR merged. A merged PR cannot
track new work, so they land as a fresh change.

P1 - the loop's actor was supplied beside its key rather than derived
from it. New() checked both were non-empty and nothing more, so a
misconfigured caller polls offers under actor B's eligibility, signs
every act as actor A, and writes liveness under B. The classifier keys
the observation stream by the holder, so it reads silence from a worker
that is working. Fix: derive the fingerprint from the key; drop the
parameter, so there is nothing to disagree through.

P1 - a claim reaped between the take's push and the post-claim read
turned ordinary contention into an error. Orient succeeds but reports
no window; the loop ignored Holds() and reserved anyway, which refuses,
and the park after it refuses too for want of an active claim. The
build plan's middle convergence arm is exactly this case: a refreshed
position-stamped read showing the act is no longer owed. Fix: treat the
missing window as idle before attempting further acts.

P2 - claim take is a declared liveness source in the shipped
implementer manifest, but observe() ran before the post-claim Orient
populated the fence. First iteration: dropped for an empty fence. Later
iterations: attributed to the previous claim's fence. So the claim's
own liveness was never observable under its own window, which is
exactly when a worker is most likely to stall. The claim result already
names the fence it opened. Fix: adopt it before emitting.

P2 - packet temp files were never unlinked. An unattended lane leaves
one per completed or parked iteration, leaking the host's temporary
storage and the packet contents, which are work product rather than
scratch. Fix: remove after the verb has consumed it, on every path.

All four fixes are implemented and mutation-checked already (each
reverts to a failing drill). Two drills had to be corrected as part of
it: the e2e liveness assertion hard-coded a shorter list copied from a
unit fixture and passed only because the fence bug meant claim take
never emitted, and the fence drill's pre-claim read supplied a window
it should not have had, so it passed without the fix.

Coverage needs attention: the new error paths dropped the gate reading
below 90 on the branch where they were written.

Review finding on #183, deliberately not taken there because plans/os-fa69345e.md D3 decided the opposite in advance ('the drill pins it so a future consistency cleanup does not extend the stamp there'). This card is that cleanup, made deliberate.

The tension is real. next/spec/envelope.md says position is 'the ledger position the response was computed at' and that 'every response that reached the ledger stamps it', reserving null for 'a refusal raised BEFORE a tip was ever read (a malformed invocation, an unreadable ledger directory)'. A show --position scan that read record 0 and then failed parsing record 1 reached the ledger; it simply never reached the tip.

And the tree already has a precedent on the other side: runLedgerVerify stamps fail.Position, so a corrupted chain gets the FAILING position, asserted by TestLedgerVerifyFailureExitCodes ('verification refusals are position-stamped envelopes'). show's chain_invalid is the only chain failure that stamps nothing.

D3's argument was that 'the count it reached is a count of records read before an error, not a statement about the chain'. That is right about a COUNT and wrong about the field: the stamp is documented as where the response was computed, not as the chain's length. Under that reading, verify's behaviour is the conformant one.

The change is small and needs no ledger change. runLedgerShow already tracks count inside the Records callback, and store.Records returns the ParseRecord error BEFORE invoking the callback for that position, so for a failure at position p the callback ran for 0..p-1 and count == p exactly. The failing position is already in scope; it just is not stamped.

Scope: next/cmd/seed/ledger.go (one return), next/cmd/seed/ledger_test.go (invert the D3 assertion added by #183), and a sentence in next/spec/envelope.md if the 'before a tip was ever read' wording needs sharpening to say 'before any position was read'.

id: os-4eaf8b13
title: 'next: the coverage flake looks deterministic because go test caches the bad profile'
state: cancelled

created_at: "2026-09-01T13:12:43Z"
updated_at: "2026-09-01T20:49:05Z"
---

The nondeterministic coverage-counter loss (os-cafba959) LOOKS DETERMINISTIC when go test's result cache is warm, and that is what makes it dangerous rather than merely annoying.

Observed 2026-09-01 while implementing os-cf1c9688: `make check` reported "coverage 87.4% is below the 90% gate" three times in a row, identical to the tenth of a point. That reproducibility is what a real regression looks like, and it is why I initially concluded the drop was real and went looking for the code that caused it. Cold-cache runs of the same tree immediately afterwards gave 86.7%, 90.7%, 90.7%.

The mechanism: `go test` caches a package's result INCLUDING its coverage profile contribution. Re-running `make check` without clearing the cache replays the same merged profile, so a run that lost a package's counters keeps losing them, at the same number, indefinitely. The earlier sighting shows the same signature: 73.1%, 73.1% (both cached), then 61.5% after `go clean -testcache`.

Consequences for whoever takes os-cafba959, and for anyone diagnosing a coverage red before then:

1. "Re-run before believing it" is only sound if the re-run is COLD. `go clean -testcache && go test ...` is the discriminator; a bare re-run of `make check` proves nothing.
2. A stable coverage number across warm re-runs is NOT evidence the drop is real. Distinguishing a real regression from this flake requires several cold-cache runs, and the tell is variance (86.7 / 90.7 / 90.7), not repetition.
3. Whatever fix os-cafba959 lands should be validated cold-cache and repeatedly, or it will appear to work for the same reason the bug appears to be real.

This is a note on os-cafba959 rather than a separate defect; filed as its own card only so the diagnostic guidance is findable by someone hitting the red rather than buried in a PR thread. Close it with os-cafba959, or fold this text into that card and close this one.

title: 'next: at 200 writers, one storm pushed a chain whose new record cited a stale tip (bad_prev refused by the hook, not retried), once in three runs, across midnight UTC'

Found by the target-scale contention benchmark (os-a00d3f34) on 2026-09-03/04, the second of three 200-writer storms on a 4-core Linux host (seed perf run --writers 200 --history 40, the seed-admit hook enforcing on a bare remote). Runs 1 and 3 landed every writer with no lost update (run 1: contention 970948 ms, attempts per append 51.07). Run 2 failed after 15m30s: '1 of 200 writers failed to land; the first: writer 157: push rejected by the remote (a policy refusal, not a race): remote: seed-admit: rule verify: position 558: bad_prev: prev b692fec4bc38 does not cite tip 2492338b3552 ... [remote rejected] (pre-receive hook declined)'. The hook verified the PUSHED chain from genesis (admitUpdate materializes newID): the chain held records 0..557 with 557 = 2492..., and the writer's own record at 558 cited b692... (the hash of 556). So the client built and pushed a tree containing a newer record it did not link to, and gitref.Push classified the hook's refusal as policy (not one of the race shapes), so the writer gave up instead of re-linking; the storm's no-lost-updates assertion then failed the run (correctly: a writer's append did not land).

What run 2 had that runs 1 and 3 did not: it crossed midnight UTC (23:46 to 00:02), so the history's segment was 2026-09-03.jsonl and every append after 00:00 opened 2026-09-04.jsonl (Store.segmentForAppend names the segment by the wall clock, not the record's ts). Ruled out by reading: Store.Tip reconciles from the segment scan and never trusts HEAD; segmentNames sorts, so a two-segment chain scans in order; Append re-checks prev against the reconciled tip, so the client's OWN store held tip b692 when it appended; each writer has its own git dir and index; AppendLoop uses a fresh temp dir per attempt. Not yet explained: how the pushed tree (git add -A over the temp dir with the client's persistent index, write-tree, commit-tree on the fetched tip) carried record 557 the client's store did not reconcile, or how the hook's materialization differed from the client's tree. Suspects, in order: the index entry for the newly opened 2026-09-04.jsonl from a previous attempt of the same writer (a stale blob retained by git add -A across attempts when the file's stat matches), and git archive or tar of a two-segment tree.

Expected shape: a deterministic drill first, two writers through gitref.AppendLoop against a bare remote with the ledger's WithClock crossing midnight between attempts, asserting the pushed chain verifies at the hook; then the fix where the drill points; and, whatever the cause, Push should not classify a bad_prev refusal whose cited tip is not the tip this attempt fetched as policy: it is a moved tip or a client defect, and re-linking is the loop's answer to both (loop.go's comment lists the race shapes; a hook's bad_prev at the new record's position is a seventh). The failing chain was not kept (the measurer removes its work dir); the drill should keep the pushed tree on failure. Tier: standard (gitref and ledger are the hot path; a chain violation at the door is the thing the benchmark exists to catch). Evidence: /home/user/wt/perf-200-run2-failed.log on the session host (the envelope quoted above); the storm's history and drafts carry ts 2026-09-02T00:00:00Z while the segments are named by the clock.

Implements the lane-facing surface named by the promotion amendment (plan #167, build plan Phase 9 item 5). THE IDEA: Seed represents permission (affordances, 8.1/8.2) but not OBLIGATION — nothing answers what is owed, by whom, since when, under what clock, and which verbs discharge it, although every fact is already folded (an active claim with its lease, a submission awaiting a verdict, an admitted run.started with no run.settled, a contract blocked awaiting a human, an open reservation, a red gate). THREE DELIVERABLES, one story. (1) OBLIGATIONS PROJECTION: a projection like every other — deterministic, byte-identical, position-stamped, rebuildable, NON-AUTHORITATIVE, derived from the same fold admission enforces — emitting per (subject, actor) rows of {kind, owed_by, since_position, due_at or clockless, discharged_by: [verbs]}. It invents no legality: discharged_by comes from the transition tables, so an obligation whose discharging verb is refused at the same position is the III.I row-2 bug class one level up, and gets the same regression-class treatment as 8.2's sweep. (2) SITUATION READ: seed situation --key <k> [--subject s] [--since <position>] returning one position-stamped envelope: my standing obligations with clocks, my active windows and fences, unread messages, budget headroom, and — with --since — ONLY what changed since that position, so a resuming lane pays for the delta rather than reconstructing the world (the append-only history makes this a tail read; today every cold start re-derives everything). Read-only, idempotent, no state change. (3) LOOP VERBS: the acts a lane takes, with every derivable argument derived (fence from the active window, reservation id from the budget view, base range from the repository, submission position from the fold) and every refusal raised BEFORE signing, naming the act that would succeed — the same one-rule-set principle Phase 8 landed for legality, applied to argument construction, so the CLI makes the legal act cheap and the illegal act hard to express. Scope guard: no new authority, no new source of truth, no orchestration layer, success envelopes stay terse (teaching text lives in refusals only). Plan-first (L2); the plan decides the obligation-kind taxonomy, the exact envelope shape, and which verbs the surface covers first.

Observed 2026-08-24 on os-501a29c2. 'seed task close <id>' was run without --resolution. record_review sets Review.Evidence = a.Resolution, so the review block was written with an empty evidence field. The done-consistency lint (internal/task/statelint.go lintDone) then fails with 'done without evidence (merged PR URL or no-PR artifact, D4.5/D7)'.

Blast radius: state lint reads the shared seed-state ref, not the branch, so the check-validate 'check' job fails on EVERY open PR and on main until the card is repaired. os-221f5929 (PR #58) hit this with an otherwise-green branch.

Attaching PR evidence afterwards does not help: 'seed task attach-evidence' appends to the card's evidence list, while the lint reads the review block's own evidence field. os-501a29c2 now carries ev-309dbfe7 with the merged PR URL and still fails.

'done' is terminal with no re-record verb, so the only repair is a hand-authored state-ref commit, which AGENTS.md forbids agents from making.

Fix candidates: (a) accept/close refuse when the resolution is empty and no --no-pr marker is given, so the trap cannot be entered; (b) a supported repair verb that sets review evidence on a done card, operator-class; (c) have the lint fall back to the card's pr evidence entries before failing. (a) plus (b) looks right: prevention, plus a sanctioned way out for cards already in this state.

id: os-6fd8d63b
title: 'CI: a pull request can be opened and silently receive no check runs at all'
state: backlog

updated_at: "2026-09-04T21:23:43Z"

Observed on #314 (os-f262585a) on 2026-09-04. The PR was opened at 14:49 and had ZERO check runs until 15:16, when an unrelated push finally triggered them. For 25 minutes it presented as a normal open PR with nothing red, and I reported it as ready for review on that basis.

THE EVIDENCE. check-validate.yml triggers on pull_request with no branch or path filter, so opening a PR should dispatch it. Listing runs for the branch returned total_count 0. That was not an artifact of the query: the same call against a control branch (seed/os-d63c7441-plan, a PR opened minutes later by the same actor through the same path) returned 12. Scanning the repo-wide run list confirmed the gap directly, with nothing between the push to main at 14:48 and the first os-d63c7441-plan run at 14:56, while #314 was created at 14:49. The branch had been force-pushed shortly before the PR was created, which is the only unusual thing about its history and may or may not be related.

WHY THIS IS P1. A PR with no checks is indistinguishable at a glance from a PR whose checks have not started, and mergeable_state reads "blocked" either way, which is also what an unreviewed PR reads. The failure mode is silent in the direction that matters: nothing is red, so nothing draws the eye, and the D3/D4.5 receipt and reviewer-identity gates that make a task PR trustworthy simply never ran. An agent driving a PR to green, or a human glancing at the checks tab, can conclude a PR is fine when it has been verified by nothing.

WHAT THIS CARD OWES. First, whether the cause is the force-push-then-open ordering, a dropped webhook, or something else, which needs the workflow run list and the delivery log for that window. Then a guard: the cheapest is a check that a task or plan PR carries a completed check-validate run for its head, so an absent run is itself a refusal rather than an absence. Note the guard cannot live in check-validate, because the failure is that check-validate did not run.

A workaround exists and is not a fix: any real push re-triggers dispatch. Never an empty commit.

## Comment cm-a9ff5d44 (seed-next-implementer, 2026-09-04T21:23:43Z)

Not taken this session, and why, so the next reader does not re-derive it. This is a v1 CI card on the protected workflow surface, outside the Seed scope the session worked (next/**), and its root cause needs the webhook delivery log for the window, which no agent here can read. The guard it asks for is nonetheless designable without the root cause, and this is the shape to plan: a scheduled workflow (hourly, like seed-maintenance) with pull-requests: read, checks: write and actions: read that lists open seed/* PRs, looks up check-validate workflow runs for each head SHA, and for a head with none creates a check run named check-guard on that SHA with conclusion failure and a summary saying no check-validate run exists for this head and that any real push re-triggers dispatch, never an empty commit. That makes an absent run a visible refusal rather than an absence, needs no change to check-validate.yml, and clears itself on the next push. Note (next/internal/refusals/refusals.go:120-137) appends directly after the existing tail and only truncates a short write of its own line; Load (:161-166) ignores a final unterminated fragment only while it remains the final fragment. So after a torn write (crash, full disk) leaves an unterminated fragment, the next journaled attempt glues a valid line onto the fragment and terminates the combined invalid line; Load then rejects the journal on every future read, blocking the refusal metrics the report's refusals section is built from. WHAT IT PRINTS. On any disagreement between the committed receipt and the regenerated one, seed receipt verify fails with a single line: "receipt mismatch — the regenerated receipt is authoritative (CI is the author of record, R11); the committed copy is forged or stale". It names no field.

WHY THAT IS EXPENSIVE. The receipt carries merge_base, head, plan_path, plan_sha256, diff_files, diff_sha256 and a validation array of command/exit pairs. Any one of them can differ, and the causes are entirely unlike each other: a stale plan_sha256 means the plan moved, a diff_sha256 change means the tree moved, a validation exit means a command failed in the verifying environment and not the generating one. head in particular differs on EVERY honest receipt, because the generate-then-commit sequence records head N and commits as N+1, so a reader who suspects head has to rule it out by experiment rather than by reading.

To narrow #314 I had to: run verify without --run from the branch (passed, so structure is fine); fetch refs/pull/314/merge and run verify there (passed, so CI checkout is not it); run verify --run from the branch (passed); run verify --run from the merge worktree, which is exactly what CI runs (passed); and read the check job log to get the CI coverage reading (91.6%, so not the gate). Every one of those was an attempt to learn which field, and the tool knows.

WHAT IT SHOULD PRINT. The differing keys, with both values, and for the validation array the command whose exit differed and the two exits. The message can keep its R11 sentence; it just needs the diff appended. A structured envelope field would be better still, since the verb already emits seed-envelope/0 and a machine caller has the same problem.

Note the message also asserts a disjunction it cannot know: "forged or stale". A validation command that failed transiently in CI makes the committed copy neither.

surface it orients from. A lane that has mail and cannot learn it from

The follow-on the interleaving check's plan names (plans/os-07e6e76c.md D7, "the verdict-then-merge reconciliation and racing mode are the named follow-on, filed once this explorer's shape is known, not this card's"). That card merged as #359, so the shape is known and this is filable. Charter sections extended: SEED-NEXT.md §II.8 (done is a verdict AND a reconciliation, across two systems that share no transaction, with divergence a first-class detected state) and §II.6 racing mode (duplicate execution tolerated, first verified success settles). No Part III row changes; not schedulable ahead of an open Phase 13 row.

WHAT EXISTS. os-07e6e76c built an explorer in `next/internal/gitref`: an abstract state machine whose alphabet is the append loop's own steps, walked depth-first over every interleaving for small N with memoization, properties checked at every state, and its terminal traces replayed through real clients so the model is evidence about the tree rather than about itself. Four configurations walk 18 to 1,151 states in under fifty milliseconds; the replay is the cost, not the enumeration. `internal/reconcile` already classifies divergence as a pure function of the lifecycle fold, with the evidence-grade classes named beside the record-derivable ones. Racing mode is live at seed/6: claims admit below the declared cap, each racer carries its own fence, and `internal/maintain`'s pass reaps the settled-out racers.

THE GAP, IN TWO PARTS.

1. RECONCILIATION. `verdict.rendered → merge.requested → merge.observed → done` spans the ledger and the forge, which share no transaction, and the charter calls every arrow its own event with divergence a detected state rather than a silent assumption. What exists is a classifier and tests over hand-built folds. Nothing enumerates the interleavings of a verifier, a merger and a forge that moves on its own: a merge that lands before its observation, an observation of a merge that never happened, a force-push on the target between request and observation, a verdict rendered while a merge is in flight. The property has two halves and both need saying: every class in `internal/reconcile` is REACHABLE by some interleaving (a class nothing can produce is dead code pretending to be a guard), and NOTHING ELSE is reachable (an interleaving that produces an unclassified divergence is a hole in the vocabulary).

2. RACING MODE. The settlement rule is a concurrency property: below the cap two claims coexist, the first VERIFIED success settles, later exits are claim-scoped, and the reaper clears the rest with a packet naming the settlement. `internal/maintain/racing_test.go` drives this through hand-written record sequences. Nothing enumerates the interleavings: two racers submitting at once, a racer exiting between another's submission and its verdict, a reap arriving while a settled-out racer's own exit is in flight, a second racer's verdict landing after the first settles.

WHAT THIS CARD OWES. The explorer generalized to a second and third alphabet, with the same discipline: properties at every state, and terminal traces replayed against the real surfaces so neither model is evidence about itself. The reconciliation model's steps are the four verbs plus a forge that merges, refuses and force-pushes on its own schedule; its properties are the two halves of reachability above, plus "no interleaving reaches `done` without an authentic pass" and "every divergence the model produces is one `internal/reconcile` names". The racing model's steps are claim, submit, verdict, settle, exit and reap under a declared cap; its properties are the cap, exactly one settlement, claim-scoped exits, and the reaper leaving no active claim of a settled race. Replay drives admission (`admit.Check`) for the ledger half, as the sibling drives `Fetch` and `attempt`.

The plan decides: whether the explorer becomes a shared harness (its state machine is generic over a step alphabet; the gitref one would move behind it) or is copied per alphabet, and the cost of each — a shared harness is one instrument to keep honest, a copy is one less coupling between packages that share nothing else; where each model lives (`internal/reconcile` and `internal/maintain` are the obvious homes, and the external-test-package plus export-shim pattern from os-21bf939f applies wherever the audit or a consumer imports the package under test); how the forge is modeled (a process with its own steps, or an oracle the model consults); the sizes and where they split between `make check-next` and the weekly job.

NOT THIS CARD. The append loop and halt (os-07e6e76c, done). A third instrument of a different kind: this is the same explorer pointed at two more state spaces, and if the plan finds the two halves want different harnesses, it says so and this card splits.

Found while verifying what the Phase 13 exit record (os-d63c7441) can claim. The exit record plan routing table says of III.L row 4: "judged against #273: the registry is the one verb table, every method runs the CLI own run function under the same admission, and approvals are ledger facts attributable to their signer; met if the drills say so, else re-routed with a card." This is that card: the drills do not say so.

III.L row 4 reads: "Per-verb policy governs the machine-protocol surface with attributable approvals."

WHAT #273 ACTUALLY DRILLS. cmd/seed/serve_test.go carries exactly three tests: TestRegistryMirrorsTheCLIVocabulary, TestProtocolMethodsAreTheCLIVerbs, TestServeReturnsTheCLIEnvelopeVerbatim. All three are parity assertions: the protocol surface exposes the same verbs as the CLI and returns the same envelope. Parity is III.I row 3 and it is met. None of the three asserts anything about POLICY PER VERB, and none asserts an approval attributable to a signer on that surface.

WHY PARITY IS NOT THE ROW. Parity says the protocol surface can do what the CLI can do. The row asks the opposite question: that what a caller may do THROUGH that surface is governed per verb, and that approvals granted there are attributable. Those are different claims, and the stronger one is the row. An implementation that mirrors the CLI perfectly and applies no per-verb policy satisfies every drill #273 added and fails this row.

The admission boundary does govern by verb, and approvals are ledger facts, so the row may well be TRUE. The point is that nothing DRILLS it on the protocol surface, and the exit record cites drills by name.

WHAT THIS CARD OWES. Either a drill on the serve surface showing a verb refused by policy there and an approval attributable to its signer, at which point the row flips; or, if the seam makes it structural, the record says so in the Phase 12 telemetry-grep style and the row is met by assertion with the reasoning written down.

Until then III.L row 4 stays routed rather than met, and the exit record cites this card.

## Comment cm-9df0f462 (seed-next-implementer, 2026-09-04T15:18:04Z)

Determination, so this card is decided rather than open. The row is structurally TRUE and what it needs is a drill, not an implementation.

WHY IT IS TRUE. cmd/seed/serve.go dispatch resolves the method through the same registry the CLI dispatches (reg.Resolve) and then calls g.Run(append(prefix, argv...), &stdout, &stderr) — the CLI OWN run function, with the params as its argv — and returns the seed-envelope it rendered verbatim as the JSON-RPC result. The file header states the design: "A method invocation runs the CLI own run function with the params as its argv and returns the seed-envelope it rendered, verbatim ... a refusal is a result carrying the failing envelope, never a transport error, so a machine caller reads the same structured code the exit status carries."

There is therefore no second admission path to govern. Per-verb policy governs the protocol surface for the same reason it governs the CLI: they are one code path. Approvals granted through it are ledger facts signed by their actor, attributable like any other record. An implementation could not diverge without introducing a second dispatch, which the registry seam forecloses.

WHY THE ROW STILL IS NOT MET. Nothing DRILLS it. The three tests in cmd/seed/serve_test.go are parity assertions (vocabulary, verb set, envelope verbatim), which is III.I row 3. Parity says the surface can do what the CLI can do; this row says what a caller MAY do through it is governed per verb. A refactor that gave serve its own dispatch would pass all three parity drills and silently break this row, which is exactly the gap worth a test.

THE DRILL THIS CARD OWES. Over seed serve, invoke a verb that admission refuses on policy grounds (the ceiling rule is the cleanest: an agent-kind key claiming above its squad declared max_agent), and assert the JSON-RPC result is a seed-envelope carrying that refusal code — not a transport error, and not a success. That proves policy governs the surface rather than only the CLI. A second arm asserting an approval made through the surface lands as a ledger fact naming its signer closes the attributable clause.

So the exit record can cite this card and, once the drill lands, flip III.L row 4 to met rather than re-routing it again. No design decision is needed after all; I was wrong to file this as one. What it needs is one test file, which needs this card promoted.

title: 'next: close the key-file TOCTOU between the loop''s identity check and its signing site'
state: done

author: seed-next-implementer

Deferred from the review of #196 (thread
https://github.com/shaunlmason/open-seed/pull/196#discussion_r3906512204),
verified real and deliberately not fixed there: choosing a shape from a P2
comment on a PR already in its fourth round is how a scope guard stops
meaning anything.

The window. internal/loop re-derives its actor by fingerprinting the key
file before every act (next/internal/loop/loop.go, checkIdentity). The act
itself then passes --key <path> across the CLI seam: loopdrive.go enters
run(), which reaches loopSigner (next/cmd/seed/loop.go) and reopens the
same path independently. An atomic replacement landing between those two
reads is observed by exactly one of them. The check is time-of-check, the
signature is time-of-use, and they can disagree.

Severity, stated honestly so the deferral is not convenient. The window is
microseconds between two reads in the same process and needs a rename(2) to
land precisely inside it. The outcome is bounded by the fence rule
(next/internal/admit/admit.go:190): a holder-signed event is admitted only
from the holder, so a cross-identity work act still refuses at the
boundary. What the race defeats is the loop's ability to DIAGNOSE a
rotation cleanly, not the invariant that a window is worked only by its
holder. That is why it is P2 and not P1.

Two candidate shapes, both with real costs, and picking between them is the
work:

1. Widen the loop verbs to accept key material rather than a path, on stdin
   or an inherited file descriptor. Closes the race completely: one read,
   one identity. Cost: it changes a protocol surface seven verbs share, and
   a material-bearing seam is a bigger security surface than a path-bearing
   one.

2. Have the Driver copy the key to a private path it owns for its lifetime
   and sign from that. Cheap and local. Cost: it puts private key material
   in a second place on disk, which plans/os-eb35672a.md already argues
   against for the loop.

A third option that should be considered before either: compare the
fingerprint AT the signing site instead of eliminating the second read. The
loop would pass its expected fingerprint down and loopSigner would refuse a
key that does not match. That does not make check and signature atomic, but
it moves the check to the same read the signature uses, which is the actual
defect. It costs one optional flag rather than a protocol change.

Acceptance: the chosen shape is implemented, the decision recorded in
next/docs/decisions.md with the shapes rejected and why, and a drill that
FAILS if the race is reintroduced. The drill needs a deterministic
interleaving seam, not a sleep: an injection point in the same style as
InjectPacketWriter, so the replacement is forced to land inside the window
rather than raced for.

---

Three findings from the Codex review of #173, all landed on main because the PR merged before the review was worked. All three verified against source; two are on the remote optimistic-retry path and one is a panic. Plan-first (L2).

(1) P1 — DERIVED ARGUMENTS ARE NOT RE-DERIVED AFTER THE TIP REFRESHES. loop.commit derives the payload once from openLoopSession's view, then hands the finished payload string to remoteSession.pushDraft, which re-signs and re-runs admission per attempt against the REFRESHED store but never re-derives. If a second valid reservation lands between session open and push, admission still accepts closing the originally cited reservation, because the budget rule checks only that the citation exists, is valid and is unclosed — it never requires it to be the SOLE open one. So the command silently makes exactly the choice soleOpenReservation exists to refuse. Same exposure for the fence. This is the defect plans/os-7e197768.md D3 was written to prevent ("a fence read from a stale local copy would be wrong under exactly the contention that makes claiming online-only") — the session was shared, but the derivation still ran once, outside the retry. Fix direction: derive inside each optimistic attempt against the same refreshed store admission uses, which means pushDraft taking a payload FUNCTION of the refreshed store rather than a string.

(2) P2 — A REMOTE REFUSAL IS STAMPED FROM THE STALE VIEW. loopSession.refuse recomputes affordances from ls.ctx and calls stampTip(env, ls.ctx.Count). On the remote path the refusal was computed one or more positions later, and remoteFailureEnvelope ALREADY stamps the refreshed position correctly through the refusalAt wrapper — so refuse actively OVERWRITES a correct stamp with a stale one, and advertises affordances from before the race (it can list claim.taken as legal on a subject a rival just claimed). Worse than the review states: the fix is not only to propagate the refreshed context but to stop clobbering a position the refusal already established.

(3) P2 — A JSON null PACKET PANICS THE CLI. loopPacket unmarshals --packet into map[string]json.RawMessage. The valid JSON value null unmarshals with no error and leaves the map NIL; if --base or a usable --repo then supplies a range, `parts["base"] = b` panics with "assignment to entry in nil map" (reproduced: assignment to entry in nil map). Without --base/--repo it refuses cleanly, which is why the drills missed it. A malformed packet must produce the documented usage envelope, never terminate the CLI. Fix: verify the root value is an object before mutating, and drill null alongside the existing malformed-packet cases.

Scope guard: no surface change. The verbs, flags, envelope and journal contracts stay exactly as they are; this is three correctness fixes plus their drills. The drills should include a remote contention case that proves re-derivation (a rival reservation landing between session open and push must refuse naming both candidates, not silently close one).

Found while planning os-6a08b166 (Phase 9 item 4, small-team and fleet
end-to-end fixtures), and deliberately NOT taken there: that card's
scope guard forbids widening a CLI posture from a fixtures card.

runVerdictRender in next/cmd/seed/verdict.go defines its flag set as
--ledger, --subject, --repo, --key, --verdict, --artifacts, --timeout.
There is no --remote. Every other admitted surface reaches both
postures: openLoopSession branches on --remote vs the local store, and
offer publish, seal and the loop verbs all push through remote.go's
pushDraft.

The consequence is concrete and blocks a charter row. SEED-NEXT.md
III.J's closing row requires small-team mode AND fleet mode to "both
run the full loop in CI". Fleet mode means disjoint actors per lane
against ONE shared ledger, and a shared ledger is the remote posture -
contention between two workers racing claim take needs remote.go's
optimistic AppendLoop, since ledger.Store.Append has no retry at all
and returns ErrWrongPrev the moment the tip moved. So the fleet's
verifier lane has no way to render a verdict onto the fleet's own
ledger. Small-team mode is unaffected: one principal on one machine
runs the local posture, where verdict render already works.

This is NOT a flag plumbing job, which is why it is its own card. The
verdict payload carries "submission": "<position>" - a DERIVED value,
bound by the verdict rule to s.Submission.Pos. On the remote path the
tip moves between attempts, so the position must be re-derived per
attempt and the act REFUSED rather than silently re-pointed if the
binding changed. That is exactly the seam pushDraft's recheck parameter
exists for, and exactly the defect class plans/os-9b3f3ef3.md D1
records: "a derived value is re-examined against the refreshed tip and
refused rather than replaced". Getting it wrong the obvious way - fetch
the tip, recompute submission, sign, push - would bind the verdict to
whatever submission happens to be current, which is a laundering shape.

Scope: next/cmd/seed/verdict.go (the flag set, the session, the push
path with its recheck), next/cmd/seed/verdict_cli_test.go (a remote
drill, including one asserting a verdict whose bound submission moved
mid-flight is REFUSED rather than re-pointed), and a sentence in
next/spec/verdicts.md recording that the render verb reaches both
postures and how the binding survives the retry.

Above L1: plan first at plans/<id>.md via its own PR.

id: os-a41892ac
title: 'engine: release v0.15.3 and bump the pin — the pinned receipt hash depends on the clone, so every task PR''s verify fails non-deterministically'
state: review
priority: P1
squad: core
author: seed-next-implementer
created_at: "2026-09-04T17:12:17Z"
updated_at: "2026-09-04T20:44:22Z"
---

P1 because it makes the D3/D4.5 receipt gate unusable: every task PR verify can fail on a correct receipt, and no amount of local verification predicts it. Four PRs are red on this right now (#308, #311, #313, #314).

THE BUG. seed receipt generate hashes the output of git diff verbatim. git writes "index <old>..<new>" lines using an abbreviation length it derives from the repository object count, so the SAME tree hashes differently in different clones. Demonstrated on seed/os-aaec6a3c, identical content both times:

  core.abbrev=7    62e70a6e5cfd4fc3c05fee7f
  core.abbrev=12   9076b22e5d2a3e0f84edc33a

An agent generates the receipt in its worktree; CI regenerates in its own clone and compares. The hashes disagree, and verify fails with "receipt mismatch". It cannot reproduce locally, because generate and verify share one clone there, which is why this burned several hours of misdiagnosis (a runner flake, then the stale-plan rule, then the engine pin) before the mechanism was found.

HOW THE OTHER CAUSES WERE RULED OUT. internal/receipt/receipt.go gives each failure its own message: a non-zero validation exit prints "validation command failed (exit N)", a stale plan prints "plan changed since branch base (D3 stale-plan rule)". CI printed NEITHER, only "receipt mismatch", so in CI all validation commands exited 0 and the plan was current. The mismatch switch then leaves only DiffSHA256 / DiffFiles.

THE FIX IS WRITTEN AND UNRELEASED. open-seed-engine c57e748 ("receipt: hash the diff with full blob ids, independent of the clone") adds --full-index. Source-level confirmation: v0.15.2 internal/receipt/receipt.go:88 is repo.Git("diff", mb, head, ...); main:94 is repo.Git("diff", "--full-index", mb, head, ...). It is the ONLY commit after v0.15.2, and .seed/engine.lock pins v0.15.2, so CI and every agent run the buggy hash.

WHAT THIS CARD OWES, in order:
1. open-seed-engine: bump VERSION to v0.15.3 on a PR. Merging mints the tag via the release workflow. Note this is a release action and the classifier blocked an agent from doing it unattended, so it wants a human hand or an explicit grant.
2. open-seed: bump .seed/engine.lock to v0.15.3. Protected path, so owner review regardless.
3. Regenerate the four receipts under the new engine and confirm verify passes in CI.

WHY THE PIN BUMP MATTERS BEYOND THIS. Until it lands, a green local verify means nothing about CI, and a red CI verify means nothing about the receipt. The gate is not measuring what it claims to measure.

Scope: add human-readable rendering for the read-only surface, without weakening
the machine contract.

  sorted by state then priority rather than by id. Colour only when the terminal
  supports it and `NO_COLOR` is unset.

JSON field set. This is presentation only.

- internal/loopverb, the registry of the seven acts (#188).

- What exhaustion parking does with the packet's acceptance and findings when the refusal is the only thing known.
- Whether the loop asserts its own manifest (read internal/lane, act only through the declared acts) or merely happens to agree with it. Asserting it is stronger and is the natural close of 1a's loop.

id: os-b3eeeabb
title: 'next: mint the deployment''s operator identity and re-sign the capability card (operator act, os-f11601e0 D2)'
state: backlog

OPERATOR ACT, filed by os-f11601e0 (plan #368 D2) rather than performed. An implementer must not mint a deployment's identity on the operator's behalf, so this card records the work and its constraint and waits for the operator.

WHY IT IS OWED. next/docs/decisions.md records, under "CI diffs content, not signatures": "The fixture deployment's card is signed by a throwaway key kept out of the tree." A public key cannot be derived from a SHA-256 fingerprint or from an ed25519 signature, so the signature on next/boundary/card.json is unverifiable by anyone, including its own repository. os-f11601e0 made the reader's half reachable (seed boundary verify) and made the canonical form RFC 8785, so the mechanism is sound end to end; what is missing is a key someone actually holds.

WHAT THE OPERATOR DOES. Generate the deployment's operator keypair; re-sign the card with it (seed boundary card --config fixtures/deployment/seed.json --key <the new key> --name open-seed --out boundary/card.json); check in the public half; keep the private half out of the tree.

THE CONSTRAINT THAT BINDS THE CHECK-IN (os-f11601e0 D1, next/spec/boundary.md "A key pinned in-tree is a trust anchor or it is nothing"). The public key file joins the declaration's `protected` list AND CODEOWNERS in the same change that introduces it. next/boundary/ is on neither list today. A key on neither can be swapped together with the card in one non-owner change, and a gate reading it would still pass: it would verify that the card matches whichever key the last committer supplied, which is no property at all. A key pinned without both entries is worse than no key, because it reads as a trust anchor and is not one.

ONLY THEN is a Makefile change worth making: with a protected key in the tree, `make check` can pass --pubkey-file to `seed boundary check` and the repository's gate becomes a signature gate rather than the content gate it is today. Makefile is a protected path, so that change carries owner review on its own account.

NOT THIS CARD. The canonical form (os-f11601e0, done: RFC 8785 through jcs.Transform). The reader's verb (os-f11601e0, done: seed boundary verify). The honesty pass on the content gate (os-f11601e0, done: the envelope note and next/spec/boundary.md). Nothing here changes behavior that an agent can change alone.

`seed template upgrade` resolves the target release by following https://github.com/<repo>/releases/latest and reading the redirect. That HTML endpoint 404s for a private repo even with a Bearer token (github.com HTML does not honor token auth the way api.github.com does), so with shaunlmason/open-seed private the command exits template_host_unreachable regardless of credentials.

Confirmed 2026-08-23 after publishing the v0.1.0 release (os-62b64ce8): the release is correct and api.github.com/repos/shaunlmason/open-seed/releases/latest returns tag_name v0.1.0, but the HTML redirect probe returns 404. Public control: open-seed-engine (public) redirects 302 -> tag/v0.13.2, which is why the engine bootstrap and `seed upgrade` work today.

Two candidate resolutions (pick one, they are not exclusive):
1. Make the template repo public — it is the artifact consumers are meant to pull from, and the handbook already documents pull-based upgrades against it.
2. Have the engine resolve via api.github.com with an optional token, falling back to the HTML redirect — needed anyway for anyone running open-seed from a private fork.

Also: docs/handbook.md 'Cutting a template release (maintainers)' says bump version, commit, tag that commit. It omits publishing a GitHub Release, which the resolution path actually requires — a tag alone is not enough. Update the checklist.

The filed tier is presence-only data. intent.filed requires the field
non-empty (transition.CheckCompleteness) and validates the VALUE no
further. One value carries authority:

  - Fold.CheckPlanGate exempts exactly the string "trivial", so a
    trivial-tier contract submits with no approved plan.

an unrecognized tier gets the stricter treatment at each. The residual

most untrusted text in the system, and holds least standing capability.
Capability bounds do not contain it here, because filing is its own
legitimate act. A dispatcher persuaded by "this is routine, file it as
trivial" ships a contract past two gates.

deciding what the vocabulary IS, and that is the tier/qualification

tier system (Phase 9/10)"). Inventing one from the injection card would

Found 2026-09-07 while the state ref was halted. `accept` (review -> done) enforces one precondition, `resolution_present`. It does NOT check whether `plans/<id>.md` resolves. So an operator can accept a plan-less card with a plain --resolution, and the card lands in `done` carrying evidence but no `no-pr:` prefix. The D3/D7 conformance lint then fails on it forever.

Unrepairable by design: `.seed/port-schema/transitions.json` has exactly one transition touching `done` (review -> done via accept) and its own note says "done is terminal, so no transition can repair it". Confirmed at the CLI: `task close --no-pr` on a done card returns invalid_transition; `task record-evidence --no-pr` returns evidence_already_recorded; `reinstate` is cancelled -> backlog only; the port spec declares no amend, edit or repair verb. The only remaining route is a direct edit of the seed-state ref, which AGENTS.md forbids agents and which is a protected surface.

Operational cost: `state lint --halt-on-fail` runs at :17 hourly (.github/workflows/seed-maintenance.yml), so the repo re-halts every hour and every mutating verb is refused for every actor until someone resumes by hand. Observed 2026-09-07: HALT at 06:52 after three accepts at 06:26, manual resume at 07:18, lint still failing.

Live instances (all three legitimately plan-free, all missing the flag): os-0dba8c6a (its deliverable WAS a plan PR, #319), os-5fe43832 (merged as a docs: PR, #305), os-405d3b20 (an L1 card merged from a claude/ branch, #342; its own evidence records "no receipt: the card is L1 and receipt generate refuses without a plan").

Scope: add the precondition to accept so the refusal happens while the card is still in `review` and still fixable, naming --no-pr in the failure detail (the fail_detail text already explains the exemption; it just is not enforced). Engine change, mirrored in .seed/port-schema/transitions.json (protected surface: PR + owner review). Open question for the plan: whether the lint should also treat a done card whose evidence names a merged PR as satisfying D7, which would retire the three live instances without a state-ref edit; if not, those three need an owner-side edit either way. Above L1: plan first.

---

The coverage gate in `make check` (check-next) fails nondeterministically, reporting a total far below truth on a tree that is fine. Observed repeatedly on 2026-09-01 while merging main into several branches:

    check-next: coverage 73.1% is below the 90% gate
    check-next: coverage 61.5% is below the 90% gate
    check-next: coverage 62.2% is below the 90% gate

...on trees that give a stable 90.4% on the next run, cold cache, with no change at all. Every test PASSES in the bad runs; only the merged profile is short.

This is the failure mode the Makefile's own comment already names:

    # -p 1 serializes package test binaries: concurrent binaries under the
    # subprocess-heavy drills can collide coverage counter files (same pid
    # and second after heavy pid recycling), silently dropping one package
    # from the merged profile and misreading coverage far below truth.

So `-p 1` reduced the collision rate but did not eliminate it. Diagnosis on one bad profile: the deficit is concentrated in internal/admit/admit.go, internal/admit/affordances.go, internal/obligation/obligation.go and internal/project/obligations.go, which is consistent with one or more test binaries' contributions being dropped rather than with any code change.

WHY THIS MATTERS MORE THAN A NORMAL FLAKE. The failure presents as 'your change dropped coverage 28 points', which is exactly what a real regression looks like. An unattended agent seeing it will go hunting for a coverage regression it did not cause, and the correct response (re-run once, then treat a second failure as real) is a rule it has to apply against its own instinct. That is the same argument os-c4e8b57a made for the auto-gc cleanup race, and the same reasoning applies: removing the race is cheaper than paying the diagnosis cost on every future red.

It also makes CI's verdict on any PR probabilistic, since the same gate runs there.

LIKELY FIX. Go 1.20+ supports GOCOVERDIR-based coverage collection (go test -cover with -args, or `go build -cover`), which writes per-process counter files into a directory instead of merging via the legacy -coverprofile path, and does not have the pid-collision failure mode. Alternatives: give each package's profile a distinct output path and merge explicitly with `go tool covdata`, or set GOCOVERDIR for the subprocess-spawning drills. Worth measuring the collision rate before and after so the fix is evidenced rather than assumed.

Scope: the Makefile's check-next target, possibly a small helper script, and whatever the drills need so subprocess re-execs do not collide. No production code.

files.tasks/os-d82cd66c.md:
---
id: os-d82cd66c
title: 'the frontier''s status words drift: twenty stale claims in next/docs/progress.md, and nothing checks them'
state: backlog
priority: P2
squad: core
created_at: "2026-09-07T07:19:41Z"
---

Found by review on #364 and confirmed by a sweep: `next/docs/progress.md` carried twenty status claims and every one was stale. Sixteen item lines read **in review** for cards long since done and closed, one still called a merged PR a draft, three prose claims said the same of merged work, and one said a card still stood at the gate. The oldest had been wrong since Phase 10. #364 fixed all twenty by hand; this card is about why they went wrong and stayed wrong.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN A DOC NIT. AGENTS.md makes this file the single resume point: "A fresh agent resumes from this file alone", and "never start new work while it misstates the frontier". Its own closing paragraph then says "If an open task PR is red or carries review feedback, drive it green first, nothing merges out of order." So sixteen false in-review lines do not merely read wrong: they route a fresh agent into finished work, ahead of the actual frontier, under a rule that tells it to prioritise exactly those lines. A drift of one entry is noise; a drift of twenty makes the resume point worse than no file.

WHERE THE STALENESS IS BORN, EXACTLY. `.github/workflows/seed-maintenance.yml` already closes merged task PRs on its hourly tick ("Close merged task PRs (accept + cascade after merge)"): it walks `review` cards, finds the merged `seed/<id>` PR, and calls `seed task close`. That step is the precise moment a `**in review**` line in the progress file becomes false, and the loop is already standing there holding both facts (the card just moved to done, and the PR number it merged as). Nothing looks at the doc.

WHAT THIS CARD OWES. A check that makes the truthfulness rule real instead of stated. Shape, as far as this card fixes it: read the status claims out of `next/docs/progress.md`, resolve each to its card on the seed-state ref, and report every line whose claim disagrees with the card's state and review evidence. The card record is the authority (state plus the server-attributed evidence URL its close recorded), never a git-log grep: this session's clone is shallow and absence in the log read as a missing merge, which is how a naive version of this check would produce confident nonsense.

THREE CONSTRAINTS THE PLAN MUST RESPECT, EACH ALREADY VISIBLE.

1. IT MUST NOT HALT. `seed state lint --halt-on-fail` writes the HALT marker, and that consequence is calibrated to state-ref integrity: a forged accept, a rewritten log, a card claiming done with no merged PR (design-options D7, R10). A stale sentence in a document is not a forged accept and must not stop the queue. This is report-grade or a soft gate on the PR that touches the file, and the plan should say which and why. Conflating the two would make the HALT marker mean less, which is a real cost paid for a doc lint.

2. IT IS REPOSITORY-SPECIFIC, NOT A TEMPLATE OR ENGINE FEATURE. No adopter has a `next/docs/progress.md`; that file is this repository's own Seed-implementation frontier. So the check belongs to this repo's loop, not to `scripts/seed` (which ships to adopters) and not to the shipped template. The plan picks the home and states the boundary it respects: the ground rules limit Seed's v1 integration points to the Makefile and the docs tree, and a check that reads a `next/**` doc while consulting the v1 state ref sits across that seam. Naming which side owns it is most of the design.

3. DETECTION AND CORRECTION ARE DIFFERENT ASKS. Flagging is cheap and safe. Auto-editing the prose is not: the file's entries carry a long parenthetical of substance after the status word, and two entries in it are legitimately not flat. os-29e2fef2 is a genuine mixed case (task PR merged, card still in review), and the Phase 13 record's aside reads "in review AT THIS RECORD'S WRITING", which is historical narrative that is true as written and that an eager rewriter would falsify. Any correcting variant must distinguish a live status claim from a record of a past moment. The plan may reasonably scope this card to detection and leave correction to a follow-up, and should say so rather than leave it implied.

WHAT WOULD MAKE IT WORTH LESS. If the check only runs on PRs that touch `next/docs/progress.md`, it catches nothing: the failure mode is a card merging and NOBODY touching the file. It has to run where the frontier moves, which points at the maintenance tick beside the close step, or at a gate every PR passes.

NOT THIS CARD. Rewriting the file's structure, or generating the frontier from the cards wholesale. The file's value is its prose, the parentheticals recording what each card actually did and why, which no generator produces; the status word is the only part that should have been derived and was not.

Found while verifying what the Phase 13 exit record (os-d63c7441) can claim.

III.A row 7 reads: "Erasure obligations are honorable: erasing a referenced artifact never breaks chain verification, and the erasure is itself an attributable event."

HALF OF IT IS DRILLED. TestSealEndToEndCLI (cmd/seed/seal_cli_test.go) removes a sealed ciphertext and asserts the maintenance pass reports seal_evidence_missing, twice over; cmd/seed/seal.go words it "erasure is a surfaced state, never silence". internal/artifact/artifact.go says the same of the sealed bucket: "deleting one is the charter erasure path, surfaced by the audit, never silence".

THE OTHER HALF IS ABSENT BY CONSTRUCTION. "The erasure is itself an attributable event" means a record in the chain, signed by whoever erased. There is no erasure verb: a grep for a Verb constant matching eras/delet/redact/forget/tombstone across internal/ returns nothing, and admit CatalogVerbs drafts none. What exists is a maintenance LINT FINDING, which is a projection of absence, not an attributable event: it says the ciphertext is gone, never who removed it or when. A lint finding also cannot be verified by a fresh reader from the chain alone, which is what "attributable" buys.

The first clause is arguably structural: the chain hash-links records and references artifacts by digest, so erasing artifact bytes cannot break verification. It is still undrilled. A cheap drill would erase an artifact and assert ledger verify stays green.

WHAT THIS CARD OWES A DECIDER. Either (a) add the erasure verb so the act is a signed record and the row is met, which touches the protocol and the transition table and is not small, or (b) revise the row the way the Phase 10 record revised its criterion, saying erasure is surfaced rather than attributed, and say so in the exit record. Not decidable from the tree: the charter wrote "attributable" deliberately.

Until then III.A row 7 cannot be flipped to met by the exit record, and the record should say UNMET and cite this card.

title: 'seed: a blocked card cannot gain a second blocked_on entry, though the model and the unblock path both expect several'
state: backlog

created_at: "2026-09-04T11:57:56Z"
---

The card model treats `blocked_on` as a list and the unblock path drains it one entry at a time: `PlanUnblock` removes the `plan:<pr>` entry and only moves the card to `ready` when the list is empty (internal/task/maintain.go). So a card blocked on two things is a state the engine expects to exist.

Nothing can create it. The transition table (.seed/port-schema/transitions.json) carries exactly two edges into `blocked`, both from another state: `ready -> blocked` (verb block) and `in_progress -> blocked` (verb transition), each with the `add_blocked_on` effect. There is no `blocked -> blocked` edge, so a card that is already blocked refuses a second entry with `invalid_transition`.

Hit today on os-88df7ab2: the card was parked on `plan:309`, and its real second blocker (dep:os-b86dab4c, whose #306 renames the verb the card's switch reads) could not be recorded. The dependency had to live in the plan and in a card comment instead of in the field the ready queue actually reads, which means `seed task ready` would offer the card the moment its plan merged, while the dependency still held.

Expected shape: one `blocked -> blocked` edge with the `add_blocked_on` effect, in the operator class beside `block`, so the entry can be added without the card leaving `blocked` or losing the entries it has. The contract is data, so the change is the table plus the engine's mirrored copy under internal/spec/testdata and a round-trip drill that a card blocked twice needs both entries removed before it is ready. title: 'next: Phase 10 — Wasteland stamps as a design reference for qualification tuples and verdict calibration'
state: backlog

---

Research note, filed as a reference for Phase 10 (deps: 9), not as a dependency. Steve Yegge's Wasteland (gastownhall/gastown, federated over Dolt/DoltHub) has shipped a working version of the thing Phase 10 has to build: a shared wanted board where rigs post work, claim it from other towns, submit completion evidence, and earn portable reputation as multi-dimensional STAMPS — quality, reliability, creativity, each scored independently WITH A CONFIDENCE LEVEL — under a "yearbook rule": you cannot stamp your own work. Verbs: gt wl browse / gt wl claim <id> / gt wl done <id> --evidence <url>, with validators reviewing submissions and evidence carried as DoltHub pull requests.

Three things worth reading it for when Phase 10 items 1 and 2 are planned. (1) Multi-dimensional-with-confidence is a different shape from a single qualification scalar, and III.E/III.G both want dimensions (tuples) and calibration (confidence); a shipped taxonomy is cheaper to critique than to invent. (2) The yearbook rule is Seed's L1 independence arrived at socially: Seed already enforces the stronger form at admission (exit 17 not_independent against ANY implementing key on the contract, past or present, verified rather than agreed), which is a positioning argument and a sanity check that the constraint is the right one. (3) Portable reputation across federated instances is a question Seed has not asked: qualification today is per-ledger standing in one keyring, and whether a tuple means anything outside the ledger that minted it is a real design question a later phase may want, or may want to refuse deliberately.

Scope guard for whoever plans against this: it is a REFERENCE, not an interop obligation. Nothing here proposes federating Seed, adopting Dolt (the ledger is a signed total order; Dolt's merge semantics are right for a many-writer reputation database and wrong for that), or importing a vocabulary. Adjacent context: this repo already depends on beads (bd) and ships a beads backend adapter, so the ecosystem is not foreign.

Sources: github.com/gastownhall/gastown; blog.kilo.ai/p/gas-town-ga. Gas City is the Kilo-hosted Gas Town, not a separate architecture.

Review finding on #168. runLedgerShow with --position <missing> opens the ledger, scans it successfully, and then returns not_found (next/cmd/seed/ledger.go, the found == nil branch) WITHOUT setting Position — although the scan established a count, so the position exists and is known. That contradicts the envelope rule (a response stamps the position it was computed at whenever one was established; only responses that never established a position carry null) and it costs the caller the very thing the field exists for: without the stamp, a caller cannot tell whether the position they asked for might have appeared concurrently. Fix: track the count during the existing iteration (no second scan) and stamp it via the shared stampTip helper on the not_found return; an empty chain establishes no position and correctly stays null. Leave the chain_invalid branch alone — a failed scan establishes no trustworthy count, and null is the honest answer there. Add a CLI drill asserting the not_found envelope carries the tip ordinal and that the empty-ledger case stays null. Note: runLedgerShow does not call journalAttempt, so stamping here does not turn a read surface into a journaled admission attempt. Recorded as a named deviation in the Phase 8 exit record (#168) rather than glossed; this card discharges it. Plan-first (L2).
